<reason>CON won by immediately reframing the clash around causation ("feet, not pixels") and turning every one of PRO's own examples into evidence that capacity tools, not geotag limits, did the work. When PRO retreated to "complements, not rivals," CON correctly narrowed the question to "what does the complement add, and at what cost," and PRO never supplied a case where promotion limits demonstrably reduced traffic, instead calling the request "rigged." CON's toothless-or-sweeping fork also landed: PRO conceded the motion "reaches the selfie," which CON used to show the tool is both broader and weaker than advertised, while drawing a principled line between a destination's own promotion (Amsterdam) and editing others' posts. CON answered PRO's gateless-site pressure with concrete, plausible tools (freeway exit closure, shuttles, fences, parking ordinances). PRO's best moves—the reversibility frame, the "tag not tagger" reframe, and the cost comparison of a blurred pin versus fences and tow trucks—were real but never overcame CON's point that a cheap tool that stops no feet delivers no benefit. PRO also underused CON's partial concession that destinations may limit their own promotion, which was arguably within the motion. Both sides had clipped turns; CON made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 [B2.2]-[B2.5]: seizing PRO's own "below carrying capacity" standard to show a cap hits the number with certainty while a blurred pin merely hopes, then forcing the commercial-scale vs. every-tagged-photo fork that PRO later conceded in [A4.2].</best_rebuttal>
